tools.change: Two things. The published severity bands themselves could not be read (the paper sits behind a page that refused the reader). Remove the bands or have a dermatologist set them. (2) The weights are those for a patient aged 8 or over only; the screen says so, but nothing stops its use for a younger child, where the result would be wrong. SECOND PASS. The instrument's own user guide has a second set of region multipliers for children under 8; the tool never asks the age and always uses the set for 8 and over. The example worked there: a young child with severe eczema of the head and neck only is given 7.2 where the guide's multiplier gives 14.4. Ask the age, or refuse a patient under 8. The live restriction page again answered "Cannot find restriction". Example: an EASI of 20.0 reads "Moderate" here and meets the subsidy's criterion for severe disease. tools.change: MISLEADING HERE. The tool averages four frequencies (0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz) and calls up to 25 dB "within normal limits". The Australian Government hearing program works with a THREE-frequency average (0.5, 1 and 2 kHz) and sets its minimum hearing loss threshold at 23.3 dB, so a patient the program counts as having a hearing loss can read "within normal limits" on this screen. The scale the tool cites (Clark 1981) also has a "slight" grade from 16 to 25 dB that the tool folds into "normal". Which average and which grades Australian audiology uses must be set by a local audiologist or ENT surgeon; until then show the average without a grade. Audiologists (a clinic role) do not see the tool at all today. SECOND PASS. (1) The program's rule was read on a second program document (the Minimum Hearing Loss Threshold guidelines, effective 1 July 2022): a three-frequency average at 0.5, 1 and 2 kHz of 23.3 dB or more, each ear by itself; a client below it can still qualify with a high-frequency average of 40 dB or more at 2, 3 and 4 kHz. Example: all four thresholds at 25 dB give "Within normal limits (up to 25 dB)" on this screen, while the three-frequency average of 25 dB meets the program's minimum hearing loss threshold. (2) No grade table from the audiologists' body or from Hearing Australia was found by search. The one Australian table read is in a Senate committee report (citing Access Economics, 2006): for adults it begins "mild" at 25 dB and "moderate" at 45 dB, with other limits for children. Those are not the tool's grades. The national data standard for degree of hearing impairment (AIHW) refuses automated readers. (3) From the United States second pass, for the shared code: the table of the paper the tool cites has a "slight" step from 16 to 25 dB, and the tool flags a difference between the ears at exactly 15 dB where the one source read there (a US academy) speaks of more than 15 dB. No Australian source for the asymmetry flag was found. Verdict unchanged: show the average without a grade until an Australian audiologist sets the grades, and offer the three-frequency average.

tools.change: Arithmetic on numbers the doctor types, in kilograms, milligrams and millilitres; it holds no medicine and no dose, so there is no national content to check. TWO THINGS FOR OTHERS: (1) a lawyer must say whether a dose calculator is a medical device here: one of the regulator's own examples of software that is a medical device is an app that calculates insulin doses; (2) general practice sees children and would use it. SECOND PASS: VERDICT CHANGED (keep to revise). THE TOOL IS ON IN AUSTRALIA AND WRITES TRAILING ZEROS. The kit prints a fixed number of decimals (read in its number-writing code today): for a child of 16 kg at 10 mg/kg for one dose, with a liquid of 160 mg in 5 mL, the screen shows "160.00 mg" and "5.0 mL". The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care's national recommendations on medicines terminology (November 2024) say not to use trailing zeros ("use '5' not '5.0'"), because 5.0 can be read as 50. Print results without trailing zeros. ROUNDING: the tool rounds a volume to 0.1 mL; no Australian source read states a rounding step (the Commission's document has none; the National Prescribing Service's sheet on measuring liquid medicines for children has none). MEDICAL DEVICE QUESTION, still for a lawyer: the regulator's document on excluded software (July 2024) describes a calculator as excluded when it calculates from published clinical standards or authoritative sources, or shows its working so that the user can check it, and does not control the giving of a dose; its page on clinical decision support says that exempt software is still a medical device, with a notice to the regulator and other duties. This audit does not say which applies to this tool.

kitGaps.gap: One shared tool list for five countries
kitGaps.detail: An English-speaking pack takes the whole shared list and may only switch a tool OFF (`araclar.kapali` in `countries/au/ayarlar.ts`). The shared test (`countries/_dil/en/testing/paketSinamasi.ts`) requires that the switched-on tools equal the shared list minus the closed ones, plus exactly two. So Australia cannot have a tool of its own (triage scale, PSA pathway, subsidy helper, hearing program), nor a slot of its own that is not a closed shared tool.

kitGaps.gap: Who sees a tool is fixed for all five countries
kitGaps.detail: `roller` is written once in `countries/_dil/en/araclar/arac1-3.ts`. Australia cannot give the inhaler check, the height tool and the dose arithmetic to general practice, or audiometry to audiologists, without giving them to the same roles in every English-speaking country.

kitGaps.gap: A country cannot state a tool's numbers
kitGaps.detail: The kit lets a pack state thresholds and intervals (`parametreler`), but the English set never passes any: `araciBicimle` returns the key, the roles and the words only, and `EnAraclarGirdisi` has no place for numbers. The eight tools whose mechanism is ready (HbA1c and TSH, bone density, viral follow-up, kidney anaemia, CRP and ESR, cardiology follow-up, bowel index, hepatitis) can therefore not be switched on in any English-speaking country even when a clinician supplies the numbers.

kitGaps.gap: A country can change only some of a tool's words
kitGaps.detail: `degisen` covers field labels, numbers, bands, warnings and the description. It does not cover the tool's name, the names of options, the dates or the line under the result, so Australia cannot rename a tool or relabel a list of choices.

kitGaps.gap: Kit arithmetic that assumes one country's convention
kitGaps.detail: Albuminuria is classified in mg/g against one grid (`kdigoA`, `kdigoRisk`): a country needs its own limits in its own unit and its own colour chart. HbA1c has one unnamed unit. The hearing average is always four frequencies with one grading. The triage tool is one scale. The radiology outline has one category list. Each needs a setting the pack states.

kitGaps.gap: The forty roles are fixed for all five countries
kitGaps.detail: Every English-speaking pack must carry exactly the forty shared role keys (the same test). Australia can rename a role (`rolAdlari`) but cannot add one (geriatric medicine, pain medicine, radiation oncology, podiatrist), remove one ("Dermatology (clinic)"), or move content between two (heart surgery from one surgical role to the other): note templates, intake questions and tool lists are tied to the key and shared.

kitGaps.gap: No way to say "this is not a specialty here"
kitGaps.detail: The landing page and the role picker group the five clinic-doctor roles under headings that read as specialties; Australia cannot reword the heading (already recorded by the earlier audit).

kitGaps.gap: The follow-up list follows the role tools
kitGaps.detail: It is given only to roles that have a tool of their own, so it cannot be a base tool for Australia.
